entries.sentence: Erection problems can have physical and psychological causes and may link to heart disease or diabetes, so a GP appointment is worth having if they persist.
entries.note: Condensed from NHS see-a-GP advice and NICE link with cardiovascular risk; causes physical/psychological per sexual health service

entries.sentence: Erectile dysfunction means trouble getting or keeping an erection, and the NHS describes it as common.
entries.note: restates sentences ledgered in body

entries.sentence: Causes can be physical, psychological or a mix, and stress, tiredness and alcohol often play a part in occasional problems.
entries.note: restates sentences ledgered in body

entries.sentence: NICE says erection problems share risk factors with heart disease and can be an early sign of it, and diabetes is another link.
entries.note: restates sentences ledgered in body

entries.sentence: The NHS advises seeing a GP or sexual health clinic if erection problems keep happening.
entries.note: restates sentences ledgered in body

entries.sentence: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for an erection lasting more than 3 to 4 hours, or for sudden chest pain that does not go away.

entries.sentence: Erectile dysfunction, also called impotence, means having trouble getting or keeping an erection.
entries.note: NHS page title and symptoms: unable to get an erection or keep one

entries.sentence: The NHS lists being unable to get an erection, and being unable to keep one long enough to have sex, as the main signs.
entries.note: symptoms listed

entries.sentence: A lower sex drive can come with it too.
entries.note: loss of libido listed as a symptom

entries.sentence: Many men have an off night now and then, and the NHS describes erection problems as common.
entries.note: ED described as common; occasional problems linked to stress, tiredness, alcohol

entries.sentence: What matters is whether the problem keeps happening, because that is when the NHS suggests getting help.
entries.note: see a GP if problems keep happening

entries.sentence: Occasional problems are usually linked to things like stress, tiredness, drinking too much alcohol or using drugs.
entries.note: occasional ED causes

entries.sentence: When problems keep coming back, a physical cause becomes more likely.
entries.note: persistent cases can have physical causes

entries.sentence: The NHS names diabetes, operations on the bowel, bladder or prostate, and low testosterone among them.
entries.note: physical causes listed

entries.sentence: Some medicines can also play a part.
entries.note: some medicines can cause ED

entries.sentence: Sexual health services describe causes that are physical, psychological or a mix of both, with anxiety, depression and relationship problems given as examples of the psychological kind.
entries.note: physical and psychological causes; anxiety, depression, relationship problems

entries.sentence: NICE says erectile dysfunction shares risk factors with cardiovascular disease.
entries.note: shares common risk factors with cardiovascular disease

entries.sentence: It adds that there is growing evidence that it can be an early sign of coronary artery disease and of disease in blood vessels elsewhere in the body.
entries.note: early sign of coronary artery and peripheral vascular disease

entries.sentence: The British Heart Foundation explains that the arteries supplying the penis are narrow, so problems there can be one of the first warning signs of narrowed arteries.
entries.note: penile arteries narrow; ED can be an early warning sign of atherosclerosis

entries.sentence: An NHS hospital leaflet on cardiac rehabilitation says erection problems can appear before angina does.
entries.note: ED can be a presenting sign of heart disease and may appear before angina

entries.sentence: Diabetes is another link, since erection problems may be the first sign of diabetes or may develop years after diagnosis.
entries.note: ED may be first sign of diabetes or develop years after diagnosis

entries.sentence: This is a main reason a GP looks at your general health and not only at the erection itself.
entries.note: links in NICE text plus GP health checks in NHS page; reasoning sentence combining the two

entries.sentence: The NHS advises seeing a GP or a sexual health clinic if erection problems keep happening.
entries.note: see a GP or sexual health clinic if it keeps happening

entries.sentence: NHS inform Scotland suggests getting in touch if the problem has lasted more than a few months, things you can do yourself have not helped, and you are bothered by it.
entries.note: more than a few months, self-help not helped, bothered

entries.sentence: A routine GP appointment is the usual route.
entries.note: routing statement

entries.sentence: It is worth telling the GP if you have a heart condition or take nitrate tablets, because one NHS leaflet says people on regular nitrate medicines must avoid some erection treatments and a GP can check this first.
entries.note: nitrate medication caution; GP can check before self-treatment

entries.sentence: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if an erection lasts more than 3 to 4 hours.
entries.note: urgent warning 3-4 hours

entries.sentence: For sudden chest pain that does not go away, or pain spreading to the arm, neck, jaw or back, NHS guidance says to call 999.
entries.note: chest pain that doesn't go away, spreading, 999

entries.sentence: A hospital leaflet says chest pain that comes and goes is a reason to see a GP.
entries.note: hospital leaflet: GP visit for chest pain that comes and goes

entries.sentence: The NHS says the doctor or nurse may ask about your lifestyle and your relationships.
entries.note: may ask about lifestyle and relationships

entries.sentence: They may also carry out health checks, such as taking your blood pressure, and examine your genitals.
entries.note: health checks incl. blood pressure, examine genitals

entries.sentence: Depending on what they find, they may refer you for further tests.
entries.note: may refer for further tests

entries.sentence: Treatment is usually described as a step-by-step approach.
entries.note: NHS trusts describe stepped approach

entries.sentence: Lifestyle changes are the usual starting point, and one NHS trust lists a healthy weight, stopping smoking, regular exercise, less alcohol and less stress.
entries.note: lifestyle modifications list

entries.sentence: Counselling or talking therapy may help with stress and anxiety, and some sexual health services offer psychosexual therapy.
entries.note: counselling for stress and anxiety; psychosexual therapy service

entries.sentence: Tablets are the usual first medicine, according to NHS trusts, and a GP or pharmacist can say whether they suit you.
entries.note: first line is tablet treatment

entries.sentence: Vacuum pumps are a device that works without medicines and are often offered after tablets.
entries.note: pumps non-drug option usually after tablets

entries.sentence: Some NHS areas supply them only to men who meet set criteria, so many men buy their own.
entries.note: trusts: funded only if criteria met, most buy own

entries.sentence: Injections, a cream and, for men who do not respond to other treatments, a surgical implant are further options.
entries.note: injections, alprostadil cream, penile prosthesis third line

entries.sentence: What is funded differs between local NHS areas, so a GP can explain what is available near you.
entries.note: eligibility and funding depends on local ICB

entries.sentence: The MHRA, which regulates medicines in the UK, warns against buying erection pills from unregulated websites, social media or messaging apps.
entries.note: MHRA warning on unregulated websites, social media, messaging apps

entries.sentence: It says such products may contain no active ingredient, the wrong amount, hidden drugs or toxic ingredients.
entries.note: may contain no active ingredient, wrong dose, hidden drugs, toxic

entries.sentence: It adds that the risks are higher for people with heart disease or high blood pressure, or who take other medicines.
entries.note: especially dangerous for heart disease, high BP, other medicines

entries.sentence: The MHRA advises using only UK-registered pharmacies, and online pharmacies in Great Britain can be checked on the General Pharmaceutical Council website.
entries.note: use UK-registered pharmacies; check GPhC site

entries.sentence: Suspicious medicines or websites can be reported through the Yellow Card scheme.
entries.note: report via Yellow Card
